title: Diane Abbott and Joani Reid readmitted as Labour MPs
summary: Both MPs have had the parliamentary whip restored following separate independent disciplinary processes
body: MPs Diane Abbott and Joani Reid have been readmitted into Labour and had the parliamentary whip restored, just under two weeks into Andy Burnham’s premiership. The party confirmed that this followed separate independent disciplinary processes, although Labour said the leadership played no role in either decision. Abbott, 72, the mother of the House of Commons, was suspended for a second time last summer after saying she did not regret comments about racism that had led to her initial loss of the whip in 2023. Reid, the MP for East Kilbride and Strathaven who was elected in 2024, voluntarily relinquished the whip in March this year. Her husband had been arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in a case linked to China. Reid has never been accused of wrongdoing. The Guardian understands from Labour party sources that Reid has never been party to the police investigations into alleged Chinese spying. Abbott has apologised after the investigation concluded. It is understood the disciplinary process resulted in her receiving a formal warning from the party. A Labour party spokesperson said: “The Labour party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and party members. The party assesses any alleged breaches of such standards independently of the leadership and political interference. “Following a process conducted under Labour party rules and approved by the independent review board, Diane Abbott and Joani Reid have been readmitted to the Labour party and have had the Labour whip restored in the House of Commons. “Diane Abbott has also apologised following the independent process coming to an end. All Labour elected representatives must be mindful at all times of their platform and the responsibilities that come with that privilege.” It is understood both investigations were carried out in accordance with the Labour rulebook and approved by the party’s independent review board. Abbott was first stripped of the Labour whip in April 2023 after writing a letter to the Observer in which she argued that Jewish, Irish and Traveller people experienced prejudice rather than racism. She apologised and withdrew the remarks, saying an earlier draft had mistakenly been submitted for publication. Following a long investigation – which ended after dozens of MPs, Labour members and even some celebrities called for her to be reinstated because she apologised – Abbott had the whip restored just before the 2024 general election. The Hackney North and Stoke Newington MP completed antisemitism awareness training and received a formal warning. But she was suspended for a second time last July after she told the BBC: “Clearly, there must be a difference between racism which is about colour and other types of racism because you can see a Traveller or a Jewish person walking down the street, you don’t know. “I just think that it’s silly to try to claim that racism which is about skin colour is the same as other types of racism. I don’t know why people would say that.” Her second suspension last summer was seen as the latest sign that the then prime minister Keir Starmer intended to take a tougher approach to party discipline, after being forced to U-turn over controversial welfare cuts because of a massive rebellion by his MPs. Reid, 39, stepped aside from the Labour party in March after her husband, David Taylor, was arrested by counter-terrorism police. At the time, she said she was not under investigation, had done nothing wrong, and was voluntarily relinquishing the whip to avoid becoming a distraction while Labour carried out its own inquiries. Burnham has told Labour MPs he will change disciplinary culture and allow MPs to speak about their disagreements without fearing retribution from party whips. A government source told the Guardian that Abbott’s readmission had nothing to do with Burnham’s regime change, and that if she repeats these comments, or makes antisemitic remarks, “she’ll have to go again”. In a statement posted to her X account on Thursday, Abbott said: “Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process, I have been readmitted to the Labour party. “I have been issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted. By inadvertently referring to the Israeli Defence Force as the ‘Jewish Defence Force’, I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community. “I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it. “I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all its forms.”

title: Middle East crisis live: Iraq says it had ‘no prior knowledge’ of US-Saudi attacks
summary: Iraqi prime minister postpones trip to Saudi Arabia after attacks as government spokesperson denies Trump’s claim that strikes were coordinated with Iraq
body: Donald Trump has claimed his Board of Peace has reached an “historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza”. The US president just posted on his Truth Social platform: This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people. At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks. Trump, who chairs the international group, said the agreement “will be carried out in carefully structured phases”. As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbors. Trump also asserted in his post: The threat that emerged from Gaza on October 7 will NOT be allowed to rebuild! Under this agreement, Gaza will finally be in the hands of a new Palestinian government that serves its PEOPLE. Donald Trump is claiming his Board of Peace has reached an “historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza”. More on this in a moment. Oil prices have settled lower after a volatile session as traders digested proposed plans for a Saudi-led maritime coalition to boost defence cooperation around the Red Sea. Brent futures settled down $1.71, or 1.88%, at $89.03 ⁠a barrel on Thursday. Trade was choppy and Brent touched a session high of $93.31 after the US and Iran traded strikes on each other’s military targets again, Reuters reports. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled down 87c, or 1.03%, at $83.59, after hitting a high of $85.94. Tehran-aligned Houthi militants in Yemen last week declared a naval ⁠blockade on Saudi Arabia, threatening the Red Sea route for its oil exports, an alternative to the largely blockaded strait of Hormuz. A partner at Again Capital, John Kilduff, said: There is this sense that there is a lot of supply waiting to hit market once all of this is resolved, and that ‌is a weight against any kind of dramatic ‌price rise. Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has shared this statement on X: The United States soils its hands with a new crime every day; the terrorist attack on the residential homes of civilians on Qeshm Island is a continuation of the atrocities in Minab and Lamerd. Americans have grown accustomed to making up for the slaps they receive on the battlefield by spilling the blood of the innocent. They will pay the price. At least 175 people – most of them children – were killed on the first day of the war when a Tomahawk missile hit a girls’ elementary school in the southern Iranian city of Minab. A preliminary US military investigation found that American forces were responsible. But while reports suggest that a secretive probe into the attack has concluded, some critics fear the Pentagon will bury the results under classifications to keep the worst mistakes secret from the public. That same day, a strike hit a sports hall in Lamerd, also in southern Iran, killing at least 24 people, including teenage girls playing volleyball. The US was reportedly responsible for that too. Egypt’s government said on Thursday that authorities were analysing drone fragments from an unprecedented strike on one of its Mediterranean ports, after president Abdel Fattah al-Sisi warned of regional escalation, AFP reports. His government had earlier confirmed that a fire the day before on two gas vessels in the Damietta port – one of which was US-owned – was a result of a drone strike, the first to target the country since the outbreak of the war. Officials have struck a cautious tone in the aftermath, warning against both regional “escalation” and “speculation”. In his first statement addressing the strike on Wednesday, al-Sisi warned of the “danger of regional escalation”, in a call with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez. Authorities were carrying out an ongoing investigation into the strike, after “technical teams boarded the ship and examined the remains of the drone, which security agencies are currently analysing and studying to establish with certainty its origin”, prime minister Mostafa Madbouly said. The drone strike, similar to others that have hit Egypt’s Gulf and Arab allies throughout the US-Israeli war against Iran, has not been claimed by any warring party. Iraq’s prime minister will postpone a trip to Saudi Arabia in light of US-Saudi attacks that killed at least 20 members of the country’s Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces, Al Jazeera reports, citing a government spokesperson via the Iraqi News Agency. Haider al-Aboudi said Baghdad “has not granted any approval for attacks on specific sites or groups within Iraqi territory”. “The government had no prior knowledge of the attacks on Iraqi territory,” he added. It comes after Donald Trump claimed the strikes were coordinated with the Iraqi government, despite Baghdad’s condemnation on Wednesday. Iraq has also said it wanted evidence regarding the launch of alleged attacks on Saudi Arabia from Iran-backed groups in its territory, a demand for which al-Aboudi said Baghdad had contacted Riyadh. The Saudi defense ministry said this week that drone strikes launched from Iraq had targeted its critical infrastructure and Riyadh on Monday and Tuesday. “No party has provided any evidence to substantiate these claims so far,” the Iraqi prime minister’s spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi news agency, in comments reported by CNN. “The government will not tolerate any unilateral actions originating from within Iraq, while at the same time it will not accept any violation coming from outside its borders,” al-Numan added. As we reported earlier, earlier on Thursday Iran’s IRGC said it struck the US-run Azraq base in Jordan in response to the latest US strikes that were carried out overnight. “With the help of God, the aggressor will be punished today,” the IRGC said earlier ‌in a statement carried by state media. Three IRGC members were killed in the northwestern Zanjan province, while a toddler and their parents were killed on the island of Qeshm, in the strait of Hormuz, state media reported. And Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has said that Egypt’s security “of utmost importance” to Tehran. He wrote on X: Egypt is an important friend and partner in the region, and its security is of utmost importance to us. We must all be vigilant against Israeli plots and false-flag operations designed to undermine regional peace. The threat is clear, mutual, and fearful of Muslim solidarity. It comes a day after a drone attack saw a fire break out on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta. It was the first time Egypt has been attacked since the Iran war started in late February and signalled a potential widening of the conflict. In his post, Araghchi appeared to suggest the attack was an Israeli false-flag operation. Egypt’s prime minister Mostafa Madbouly said on Thursday that Egypt has secured alternatives to cover its energy needs after the attack. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities are continuing their investigation, he added. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei has shared this statement on X: The criminal attack last night on the homes of the noblest Iranians in Qeshm, which resulted in the destruction of several houses and the martyrdom of a hardworking taxi driver, Qeysar Jafari, his wife Zahra Jafari, and their innocent two-year-old child, Sina, pains the heart of every conscientious human being. These crimes, which evoke the terrorist actions of ISIS and are carried out under the guise of “peace through force” with the aim of punishing a nation for insisting on its rights, dignity, and independence, will never produce authority or credibility for the criminals. With every explosion, with every crime, with every sanction, with every threat, with the killing of every child, you only make Iranians more determined and united in defending their homeland. Iranian residents, mostly the fishermen community living on Qeshm Island, described waking to a series of powerful explosions at around 3.45am local time, when at least three huge strikes rocked the strategic island in the strait of Hormuz. “The first blast shook the roof sheets and rattled the doors, waking everyone up from the sleep,” one resident told the Guardian, speaking on condition of anonymity. “By the second and third explosions, the whole neighborhood was outside, and there were killed near our neighborhood. Fishermen, women, and children gathered in groups, calling relatives and trying to understand what had been hit. No one could go back to sleep.” Another resident said the strikes had left the community living in constant fear. “You never know if it’s over after one strike or if another is coming in minutes. Every loud noise now makes people panic and feel threatening,” he said. “Residents remain outside the rest of the night checking their phones for updates and news, making sure their families are safe. Everyone is frightened because we don’t know what will happen next; we are still outside our homes sitting in groups.” In the UK, the co-founder of Palestine Action has won permission to challenge the ban against the group at the supreme court. The direct action group was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July last year but its co-founder, Huda Ammori, has been fighting to have the ban overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign. In February, the supreme court ruled that the ban was disproportionate and unlawful but its decision was overturned by the court of appeal last month. On Thursday, the high court said Ammori could appeal against the court of appeal’s decision and that the case would be heard in the final quarter of this year. title: Mandela Barnes drops out of high-stakes Wisconsin governor’s race
summary: Former lieutenant governor says path to Democratic nomination no longer viable as democratic socialist rival surges ahead
body: Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor of Wisconsin, dropped out of the Democratic primary for governor on Thursday, upending the high-stakes contest less than two weeks before the 11 August election. Barnes announced the decision in a video posted on social media, saying he no longer saw a viable path to the nomination as democratic socialist Francesca Hong surged ahead with a commanding lead. “It’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be,” Barnes, 39, said. The Marquette Law School poll showed Hong significantly ahead of Barnes in a distant second place, with 38% compared to his 16%, having consolidated liberal support, especially among young voters, although about a third of primary voters remained undecided. Soon after Barnes’s withdrawal, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported it had sent questions to the candidate about past allegations of inappropriate behavior that had been anonymously submitted to the Wisconsin Democratic party, local party officials and others. According to the Journal Sentinel, the state party hired a law firm in 2025 to investigate the claims sent in a letter that Barnes had used his position in the party to pursue inappropriate relationships with “young adult women”. The party’s internal review and outside investigation found no actionable evidence because the claims were “anonymous and unspecific”, the Journal Sentinel reported, citing an unnamed person familiar with the matter. Barnes’s campaign denied any wrongdoing. “There are no allegations of misconduct or wrongdoing against Mandela,” it said in a statement. His departure adds another twist in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin, a perennial presidential battleground that has also been at the center of national disputes over election administration since the 2020 election. He is the third Democrat to exit the race, following lieutenant governor Sara Rodriguez, who withdrew two weeks ago amid a campaign finance scandal. After Rodriguez’s exit, Milwaukee county executive David Crowley re-entered the race with the endorsement of Governor Tony Evers, who is not seeking re-election. Earlier this summer, Missy Hughes, a former state economic development director, ended her campaign. On Wednesday, a judge rejected an effort backed by the Democratic party to let voters who had already cast absentee ballots void their initial vote and vote again, over concerns that many early ballots had been cast for candidates who were no longer in the race. Crowley moved quickly to appeal to Barnes’s supporters: “There’s a place for you in what we’re building.” Evers told reporters he was surprised by Barnes’s decision to withdraw but reiterated his support for Crowley, saying he believed Crowley was the strongest candidate “even if Mandela was in”, the Associated Press reported. The Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Wisconsin is expected to face Republican US congressman Tom Tiffany, who is backed by Donald Trump. Barnes was once viewed as a rising star in Democratic politics. In 2022, rather than seek re-election as lieutenant governor, he ran for the US Senate, narrowly losing the race to incumbent Republican Ron Johnson. Rachel Leingang contributed reporting

title: Senate’s latest effort to halt Trump’s Iran hostilities fails in 49-50 vote as some Republicans side with Democrats – live
summary: Republicans senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted in favor of the motion to prevent Trump from continuing hostilities against Iran
body: The House Democratic Women’s Caucus called on Thursday for an ethics committee investigation of congressman Max Miller, an Ohio Republican and former Trump aids who has been accused of domestic abuse by his ex-wife and former girlfriend. The group’s chair, Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, and vice-chairs, Emilia Sykes of Ohio and Hillary Scholten of Michigan, said in a statement: The recent reports of domestic violence and child abuse against Representative Max Miller are deeply disturbing and Congress can’t ignore them. Allegations of violence against women and children have to be met with the utmost seriousness. We therefore call on the House Committee on Ethics to swiftly and thoroughly investigate these allegations. Every woman and child deserves to live free from fear of violence, especially within the sanctity of their own home, and we will not stop fighting until that’s the reality. The Republican congressman, 37, who represents Ohio’s seventh congressional district, has denied accusations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, as he campaigns for re-election. Moreno, a conservative policy adviser whose father is Ohio senator Bernie Moreno, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The pair have been engaged in a legal battle over custody of their child since 2024. Grisham, who held the roles of press secretary for both Donald Trump and Melania Trump at various points during Trump first term, dated Miller from 2019 to 2020, when he was a White House staffer. Kathryn Ruemmler’s name appeared thousands of times in records related to Epstein, the disgraced financier and convicted sex offender, that were released earlier this year by the US Department of Justice under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The files revealed Ruemmler had accepted gifts from Epstein, who died by suicide while awaiting trial in 2019 after he was arrested by federal authorities, at times addressed him as “Uncle Jeffrey” and “sweetie” in emails, and offered him informal advice on how to respond to questions about his sex crimes. Ruemmler’s testimony before Congress when she was asked about Virginia Giuffre, a victim of Epstein’s abuse, was swiftly criticized by Giuffre’s family. “She should be ashamed of herself,” Giuffre’s brother and sister-in-law, Sky and Amanda Roberts, said in a statement. Giuffre died by suicide in April 2025. Two federal appeals courts ruled on Thursday that the Trump administration cannot deny immigrants detained inside the United States a chance for release on bond, rejecting a new policy to detain even undocumented immigrants with no criminal records who have resided in the US for years. In a pair of 2-1 decisions, majorities of the San Francisco-based 9th US circuit court of appeals and the Chicago-based 7th US circuit court of appeals agreed with four previous appeals court rulings across the country that a 1996 law does not mandate the detention of every undocumented immigrant who initially entered the country unlawfully, no matter how long ago. The majority decision in the 9th circuit court was written by Daniel Bress, a judge appointed by Donald Trump in 2019. Two appeals courts, the Fifth circuit in New Orleans and Eighth circuit in St Louis have sided with the Trump administration. The split between the circuit courts increases the likelihood that the US supreme court will eventually take up the issue, as the administration requested last month. It comes just hours after President Donald Trump said that that he may withdraw Blanche’s nomination and nominate him again after Cornyn and Senator Thom Tillis, the two current Republican holdouts, leave office in January. The State Department has announced that its limited-edition Trump-branded US passports designed to “celebrate America’s 250th” will become available on 8 August. In a post on social media, the State Department said that there will be “250,000 commemorative passports” and shared an image of the passport which appears to include a photo of Trump on the inside. According to its website, the passport, dubbed the “Patriot Passport” will include “custom artwork and enhanced images on the front, back, and inside covers.” Ahead of the vote on the latest war powers resolution, Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said that the war with Iran was “launched without a clear plan, executed without a coherent strategy and has become a costly self inflicted disaster for the American people.” “Every justification that we were given for this conflict has proven hollow” she said on the floor. Democrat Mandela Barnes has announced that he is dropping out of the Democratic race for governor in Wisconsin. In a video shared on social media on Thursday, Barnes said that “last night I had a very difficult conversation with my staff.” “We’re incredibly proud of all the things that we’ve accomplished and all the resources that we have raised to spread our message” he said. “But it’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be”. Barnes appears to be referencing state representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, who is currently leading the polls ahead of the 11 August Democratic primary. “And I said from the very beginning, when I launched this campaign that the number one goal was taking on and defeating Tom Tiffany to deliver big wins for Democrats up and down the ticket” Barnes added. “And Now, it’s time for us to come together, to focus our efforts on that one goal.” Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican of North Carolina, responded to Trump’s threat to withdraw Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general and renominate him after Tillis and Senator John Cornyn leave office in January, saying the president is “getting bad advice.” “He should listen to Blanche and others who think if it’s dead, it should be rendered completely dead,” Tillis told reporters. “That same adviser wants to bring it back to life at some point” he added. A new report alleges that billionaire Elon Musk is preparing to spend $100m to $120m on the midterm elections to help Republicans. A New York Times report on Thursday, alleges that according to two people briefed on the plans, Musk has has authorized his super PAC to spend $100m to $120m on a new field program in at least eight states to help elect Republicans in November. Musk was the biggest donor in the 2024 presidential election, spending over $240m. According to the Times, officials from Musk’s super PAC, America PAC, have communicated their nine-figure budget to Republicans in recent weeks, and that the spending plan is set to begin next month. The report alleges that Musk’s group plans to first target Senate races in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio and is also having conversations and considering spending in North Carolina, Georgia and Texas. The super PAC is also planning to spend in House races including in California, Wisconsin and Washington, according to two people familiar. On Wednesday, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer gave a speech on the chamber floor in which he implored Republicans to abandon their support of Trump’s war in Iran. “Are Senate Republicans listening? The country is clamoring for you to end this war,” he said. “I urge and plead with my Republican colleagues: listen to the American people. Vote to end this war. We’re going to keep forcing Republicans to vote until we do.” On Thursday before the vote was finalized, Schumer posted on X: Trump’s war with Iran has been one of the greatest foreign policy dumpster fires in American history, and it seems to be expanding with new attacks now targeting Egypt. Our troops’ lives are unnecessarily at risk fighting a war that was totally avoidable. All while Trump is too busy playing keyboard warrior on Truth Social. We must end this war now. A reminder that today a new poll was released on American attitudes about the US-Iran war, with most people believing this is not worth fighting. Trump’s approval rating also showed a slump, according to the new AP-NORC poll. The results are a stark repudiation of Trump’s approach to the conflict, which has dragged on far longer than he originally predicted. About two-thirds of US adults say the war with Iran has not been worthwhile, according to the new poll from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as about 37% of Republicans. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat who voted in favor of the latest war powers resolution to prevent Trump from continuing an operation against Iran, wrote on X: Senate Republicans just voted to continue Donald Trumps war with Iran for the 13th time. - Rising gas prices - Increasing grocery bills - 18 U.S. service members have been killed - Over 600 Americans have been injured We must end Trump’s war. Meanwhile, the latest attempt by Congress to rein-in president Donald Trump’s attacks in the Middle East failed in the Senate on Thursday. The war powers resolution failed in a 49-50 vote. Democratic senator John Fetterman voted with Republicans to sink the measure. But notably, Republicans senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul voted in favor of the motion to prevent Trump from continuing hostilities against Iran.
